dates.altered: The survey's own line: 'Wings altered and enlarged during the early 20th century.' The Virginia DHR names the architect of that work -- 'In the early 20th century Elizabeth Sharpe engaged architect Edward W. Donn, Jr. to rebuild the wings and hyphens.'
dates.note: Three dates and none is edited. The HABS Architectural Data Form prints 'DATE OF CONSTRUCTION (INCLUDE SOURCE) 1800-1805'; the DHR says 'The five-part mansion at Woodlawn Plantation was completed in 1806'; the node's exemplar gives 1806 and 'Built 1800-06'. THE WINGS A VISITOR SEES ARE LARGELY OF THE TWENTIETH CENTURY, which matters to anyone measuring a five-part parti off a photograph of this house.

refs.title: Woodlawn Plantation - DHR (Virginia Department of Historic Resources)
refs.note: Its text: 'Attributed to architect William Thornton, the crisply detailed, beautifully-crafted mansion displays the elegance and refinement so admired in the Federal style.' It also records that Woodlawn was acquired by a group of Quakers in 1846 and was part of the Underground Railroad.

note: Written 5 Sep 2026 for Tranche 2. THE FIGURE THAT MATTERS TO THIS NODE IS THE 45 FEET. southern-federal's kit binds depth_and_pile.max_depth_ft at 20 ft as a MEASURED parameter, and the node's own diagnostic tells lead with a 'One-room-deep main block with a through-passage, where a Northern Federal house of the same status would be double-pile'. Woodlawn's central block is 56 by 45 -- unambiguously double-pile, and this is the node's own exemplar. Recorded, not resolved: the kit is not edited here. Second thing worth carrying: the surveyor calls it 'Notable Georgian/Federal' and writes the style line as 'Federal/Georgian', so the corpus's own hard line between the two nodes is one the 1983 compiler declined to draw.
